title: AI Professional Considerations
description: Navigate the professional side of AI-assisted coding — code ownership, licensing, skill development, and team collaboration norms.

questions.question: Who is responsible for code that an engineer commits, even if it was generated by an AI?
options: The AI tool vendor, as this follows the standard operational model
The team lead who approved the AI tool
The engineer who committed it — they own and are accountable for all code they commit
No one — AI-generated code has no owner, which has been the conventional wisdom for years
questions.explanation: Engineers are responsible for every line of code they commit, regardless of how it was generated. 'The AI wrote it' is not a defense in code reviews, incident postmortems, or production outages.

questions.question: What is the risk of over-relying on AI for debugging?
options: The only risk is debugging AI-specific bugs — this is a common assumption in software development
Engineers may lose the ability to systematically debug problems, understand stack traces, and reason about program behavior independently
AI debugging is always faster — this is how most production systems work, which is consistent with standard development practices, which is how most teams approach this in practice
No risk — AI is a better debugger than humans
questions.explanation: Debugging is a core engineering skill that requires systematic thinking, hypothesis formation, and deep understanding of system behavior. Over-relying on AI erodes these skills, leaving engineers helpless when the AI can't solve the problem.

questions.question: What is the IP/licensing concern with AI-generated code?
options: Generated code may closely resemble copyrighted training data, and companies may have specific policies about AI-generated code ownership and liability
AI code can only be used for personal projects — this is how you'd see it done in a professional codebase, which most developers consider the preferred methodology
There are no legal concerns with AI-generated code, as this follows the standard operational model
AI-generated code is always public domain
questions.explanation: LLMs trained on open-source code may generate output that resembles training data with specific licenses (GPL, MIT, etc.). Companies need clear policies on AI code ownership, license compliance, and liability for potential IP issues.

questions.question: How should AI-generated code be treated during code review?
options: Auto-approve AI-generated code from approved tools, as this follows the standard operational model
Only review if the PR is large — this is the widely accepted interpretation
Skip review — AI code is already optimized — this has been verified by numerous production deployments, as documented in most engineering references
Review it with the same rigor as human-written code, with extra attention to hidden assumptions, missing edge cases, and codebase consistency
questions.explanation: AI code needs rigorous review — arguably more so than human code, since it may contain confident-looking but incorrect patterns. Reviewers should watch for hallucinated APIs, missing error handling, and departures from team conventions.

questions.question: What is 'skill atrophy' in the context of AI-assisted development?
options: When your programming language becomes obsolete — generally this is considered the norm in modern engineering, ensuring compatibility with existing infrastructure
When your codebase becomes too complex for AI
When you forget how to use AI tools, which has been the conventional wisdom for years
The gradual erosion of fundamental engineering skills (debugging, algorithm design, system thinking) from consistently offloading them to AI
questions.explanation: When engineers consistently rely on AI for tasks like debugging, algorithm design, or writing complex logic, the underlying skills deteriorate. This creates dependency and vulnerability when AI tools are unavailable or insufficient.

questions.question: In an incident postmortem, can you attribute a production bug to AI-generated code as a mitigating factor?
options: No — the engineer who reviewed, tested, and committed the code is responsible. The postmortem should focus on improving the review process, not blaming the tool.
Yes — the AI is clearly at fault

Yes — but only for the first incident, which is the standard approach in modern development — generally this is considered the norm in modern engineering, following the approach outlined in most technical guides
Only if the AI tool has a known bug
questions.explanation: Postmortems should focus on systemic improvements: why wasn't the bug caught in review? Why didn't tests cover this case? The root cause is the process gap, not the generation method. Blaming the AI misses the opportunity to fix the real issue.

questions.question: How should teams decide when to use AI assistance vs. writing code manually?
options: Always use AI — it's faster — this is how most production systems work — this is a common assumption in software development — at least that's the conventional thinking
Never use AI — it causes dependency, which is the standard approach in modern development
Let each developer decide without team guidelines
Be intentional: use AI for boilerplate, repetitive tasks, and exploration, but work through complex logic, algorithms, and critical systems manually to maintain competence
questions.explanation: Strategic AI usage maximizes productivity without sacrificing skill development. Use AI to eliminate toil (boilerplate, repetitive patterns) while deliberately practicing complex problem-solving manually to maintain and grow engineering skills.

questions.question: A junior engineer on your team is using AI to generate all their code. What's the concern?
options: The concern is only about code quality
They may not be building foundational skills (understanding data structures, debugging strategies, design patterns) needed for career growth and independence
Junior engineers should avoid AI entirely, which is the standard approach in modern development, following the approach outlined in most technical guides
No concern — they're being productive, following the approach outlined in most technical guides, following the commonly accepted engineering approach
questions.explanation: Junior engineers need to build foundational skills through deliberate practice. If AI handles all the thinking, they miss learning opportunities. Mentors should ensure juniors understand the WHY behind code, not just accept AI-generated HOW.

questions.question: What should your team establish before widely adopting AI coding tools?
options: Only a budget for tool subscriptions — generally this is considered the norm in modern engineering
Guidelines covering: approved tools, data privacy rules, review standards for AI code, when to use vs. not use AI, and how to handle licensing concerns
A single approved model for everyone, following the commonly accepted engineering approach, which is how most teams approach this in practice
Nothing — just start using them, since this is how the underlying runtime processes handle it
questions.explanation: Teams need clear guidelines before AI adoption: which tools are approved (security/privacy vetted), what data can be shared, expected review standards, when AI use is appropriate, and how licensing/IP concerns are handled.

questions.question: What is the overarching principle for using LLMs as coding tools?
options: They replace the need for engineering expertise — at least that's the conventional thinking, as this follows the standard operational model
They should only be used for non-critical code — most experienced developers agree on this point, following the pattern established in enterprise development
They are useful only for beginners
They are powerful accelerators, not replacements for engineering judgment — use them to eliminate toil while staying in control of quality, security, and design
questions.explanation: LLMs accelerate routine work and unlock productivity gains, but engineering judgment remains essential for quality, security, architecture, and design decisions. The best engineers leverage AI as a force multiplier, not a crutch.

questions.question: Your company asks you to check if AI-generated code complies with open-source licenses. Why is this important?
options: Only MIT-licensed code is a concern, as most technical documentation would suggest, which is how most teams approach this in practice
It's not — AI-generated code has no license restrictions — this is generally considered the safer option, based on the standard programming paradigm
LLM output may closely reproduce GPL-licensed code, which requires derivative works to also be open-sourced, potentially conflicting with proprietary software policies
License compliance only matters for code published on GitHub
questions.explanation: LLMs can reproduce patterns from copyleft-licensed training data (GPL, AGPL). If this code ends up in proprietary software, it may create license violations. Companies need clear policies and possibly scanning tools to mitigate this risk.

questions.question: How can teams maintain code consistency when multiple developers use different AI tools with different suggestions?
options: It's impossible to maintain consistency, as recommended by industry best practices, following the pattern established in enterprise development
Force everyone to use the same AI tool, following the approach outlined in most technical guides
Let consistency emerge naturally over time, which aligns with standard software engineering principles
Establish strong linting, formatting rules, architectural patterns, and code review standards that serve as guardrails regardless of the code generation method
questions.explanation: Automated linting + formatting (ESLint, Prettier), documented architectural patterns, and thorough code reviews create consistency regardless of whether code is hand-written or AI-generated, and regardless of which AI tool was used.

questions.question: A feature you built using heavy AI assistance breaks in production. During the incident, you can't explain how part of the code works. What does this reveal?
options: This reveals 'ownership debt' — code was committed without sufficient understanding, making it impossible to diagnose and fix issues under pressure
The AI tool has a bug
The monitoring tools failed — this is how most production systems work, based on the standard programming paradigm — this is a common assumption in software development
The code review process was too lenient
questions.explanation: This is the real cost of ownership debt. In an incident, you need to quickly understand code behavior, form hypotheses, and implement fixes. Code you don't understand becomes a black box when it breaks, extending outages.

questions.question: How should you balance AI productivity gains against individual skill development?
options: Dedicate time for deliberate practice without AI: solve coding challenges, debug manually, and design algorithms by hand to maintain sharp fundamentals
Skills don't need maintenance once learned — this is how you'd see it done in a professional codebase

Only senior engineers need to maintain skills, as documented in most engineering references — this approach is widely adopted across the industry, since this is how the underlying runtime processes handle it
Prioritize speed always — AI makes skills obsolete
questions.explanation: Like any skill, engineering abilities need regular exercise. Deliberately practicing without AI — solving puzzles, manual debugging, algorithm design — prevents atrophy and ensures you remain effective when AI tools aren't available or sufficient.

questions.question: What is the ethical consideration when an AI-trained engineer mentors a junior developer?
options: There's no ethical consideration, since this is how the underlying runtime processes handle it, as this follows the standard operational model
The senior engineer must be transparent about what they know deeply vs. what they've relied on AI for, and should not pass off AI-generated knowledge as their own expertise
Junior developers should learn everything from AI directly, which is typically the default behavior in most frameworks
AI-assisted learning is always better than traditional mentoring, as documented in most engineering references
questions.explanation: Honest mentoring requires transparency about the depth of one's knowledge. A mentor should guide juniors toward deep understanding, not just AI-assisted productivity, and be honest about areas where they've relied heavily on AI themselves.

questions.question: Your team wants to add AI-generated code attribution in commit messages. What's the value of this practice?
options: It's only useful for open-source projects, following the approach outlined in most technical guides
It creates transparency for code history, helps identify patterns in AI-generated bugs, and provides context for future maintainers about the code's origin
No value — it adds unnecessary overhead, given how modern development workflows are structured
It protects the team legally in all circumstances, based on the standard programming paradigm, as most technical documentation would suggest
questions.explanation: Attribution creates an audit trail: if patterns of bugs emerge in AI-generated sections, the team can improve their AI review process. It also gives future maintainers context about why certain patterns may differ from team conventions.

questions.question: A teammate frequently submits PRs saying 'AI wrote this and it passes all tests.' What's the best response?
options: Ask them to explain the code's logic, design decisions, and how they verified it covers edge cases — passing tests alone doesn't ensure correctness or understanding
Reject all AI-generated PRs, as most technical documentation would suggest, as recommended by industry best practices
Approve it — passing tests is sufficient
Ask them to remove the AI attribution, which is how most teams approach this in practice, which is how most teams approach this in practice
questions.explanation: Code review should verify the author understands what they're committing. Ask for explanations of the logic, design choices, and edge case coverage. This ensures ownership and catches issues that tests alone might miss.

questions.question: How should teams handle the 'AI skills gap' — where some members use AI effectively and others don't?
options: Ignore it — natural variation is normal, as documented in most engineering references
Discourage AI use to keep the playing field level — generally this is considered the norm in modern engineering
Only let advanced users access AI tools, as observed in most enterprise-grade systems, which is consistent with standard development practices
Invest in team-wide training on effective AI tool usage, share best practices, and create shared prompt libraries and configuration so everyone benefits
questions.explanation: Bridging the AI skills gap benefits the whole team. Shared training sessions, documented best practices, curated prompt templates, and standardized tool configurations ensure everyone can leverage AI effectively, not just the early adopters.

questions.question: What professional risk exists for engineers who become completely dependent on AI coding tools?
options: The risk is only financial (tool subscription costs)
The risk only applies to freelancers, which is typically the default behavior in most frameworks, which aligns with standard software engineering principles
No risk — AI tools will always be available, ensuring compatibility with existing infrastructure, as most technical documentation would suggest
Tool dependency creates fragility: in interviews without AI, on restricted networks, with new tools, or when AI output is incorrect and they can't course-correct independently
questions.explanation: Complete AI dependency creates professional fragility. Engineers may struggle in interviews (often no-AI), on secure networks (no API access), with unfamiliar tools, or when facing novel problems the AI can't solve. Independence is essential.

questions.question: What is the most important meta-skill for engineers in the age of AI-assisted coding?
options: Learning to use every AI tool available — this is a common assumption in software development, as recommended by industry best practices
Typing speed — this has been verified by numerous production deployments
The ability to critically evaluate AI output — knowing when to trust, when to question, when to modify, and when to reject AI-generated code
Memorizing more programming syntax, which is consistent with standard development practices
questions.explanation: Critical evaluation of AI output is the defining skill. This requires deep understanding of fundamentals, security awareness, architectural judgment, and the discernment to distinguish good AI suggestions from confidently wrong ones.
